utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Be seated, please. Mr. Registrar, could you have the accused brought in? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters, the translators. We are now going to resume. I hope that everybody can hear me. I can see that the Defence has prepared all its material. We are expecting a new witness. Mr. Nobilo, have you prepared a summary of the next witness's testimony, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. You have received it in writing, just as well as the Prosecutor has, the summary of the next witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment. Could I have it in French? I'm now looking at the registrar. Maybe in the future, could I have it in French? Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. That could be possible, but it simply depends in the way in which this has been presented to the registry. Has it been introduced?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. This is something that is going to become official evidence, so when the Defence is going to introduce it, it has to be introduced at the registry in such a way that the registry translates it into French so that we can more easily follow the debate. Also, that will allow me to say, "You're going out of the scope of your summary," and so on. Mr. Nobilo, please, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next witness is Brigadier Slavko Marin. He's a Brigadier of the army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and, in the relevant time period, he was the head of the operations, operatives, in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. What did his job imply? What does "operatives" mean exactly in military terms? It is much better to ask Brigadier Marin to explain his job himself. Brigadier Marin is going to speak about the structure of the HVO since the beginning of the organisation when there were crisis staffs, also, the municipal crisis committees, operational groups, then the organisation of the work of the command of the Operational Zone, the structure of the brigades and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: From the point of view of form, it is obvious that from the moment you submit a summary to us, you do not need to present it orally. That is why it was made. That is why we ask for a written summary, and that is why I asked to have it in French. But normally, each Judge will have such a summary. I do not know whether my Judges have received it. Mr. Dubuisson, maybe you could make a photocopy of the summary for each of my colleagues. Today, you can present your summary, but in the future, we can save time by not presenting the summary orally but, obviously, under the condition that we have a written summary of it previously. Maybe we can ask Mr. Marc Dubuisson or the usher to make a photocopy. Now you can have the witness introduced straight away and brought here, even though I haven't got a summary in French. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We, Mr. President, will present the witness and what we have presented in writing in the summary, but we would like to make some additions to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. You can complete it. I'm not trying to prevent you from doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Because in the last sentence of our summary, we express a reservation of saying that maybe we will enlarge, slightly, what was in the summary. This witness will speak of what happened in January 1993, because his task was to write orders and commands on behalf of General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please, I'm turning now to the Witness, could you remain standing up and tell us your name, your surname, your rank, your profession, and your address. After that, you will read the solemn declaration. Just a moment, please. First of all, can I have your name, your surname, your rank, and your address?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Slavko Marin. I come from Novi Travnik, and now I live with my family. I've got a wife and three children. At the moment, I'm Chief of Staff of the 1st Guard's Corps in Mostar, the 1st Guard's Brigade, and I'm an officer of the army of the Federation. My rank is that of Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Now please read the solemn declaration, which will be your oath. Could you please read it for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. You may be seated. You have accepted to come and give evidence here for the defence of General Blaskic who has been indicted by the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal. We have received the summary of what the Defence expects from your evidence, and now you can answer Mr. Nobilo's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, good morning. Let us go back in time, somewhere in 1991. Can you tell us, what are the first forms of organising of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina or, even more, in Central Bosnia, when the war was about to break out in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Could you please tell us, when did the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina start organising, and what were the first forms of that organisation? Could you please tell that to the Court?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. Chairman, Your Honours, before I start exploring this question, in my introduction, I will just say some basic facts which will help me to present the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the situation in which the HVO was being established, and these were the first forms of organising of the HVO in order to defend the Croatian people in Bosnia. The aggression of the Yugoslav People's Army on Bosnia and Herzegovina, first of all, on the village of Ravno, showed what the real intentions of the Serbian leadership were regarding the non-Serb populations of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That happened in September 1991. Taking into account what was happening, the political leadership of the Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina started with a series of measures and activities in order to organise the population from the forthcoming aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment. Could you speak a bit slower because of the interpreters and for the court reporters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I propose, Brigadier, is that after one or two sentences, you make a small pause, because the interpreters need at least as much as time as you need to speak a sentence. Please, could you slow down?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. So the basis was put on organising of armaments, of defining ways of organising the prevention of aggression, of finding out ways of organising the leadership structures so that the population would be organised for the defence, also, giving shelter to the refugees and displaced persons, and for carrying out other activities that were imposed on us by the everyday situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, when do first forms of organised defence appear, and what were the names of the first bodies organised by units of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: In such conditions that I've just described, as from August onwards, August 1991, crisis staffs were being organised at the level of municipalities and also of local communes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, who appoints a crisis staff and who are its members?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The membership of crisis staffs were as follows: Political representatives of local communes and municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to you, were crisis staffs military bodies or political bodies of executive authority?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: According to their structure and in view of their members, those were more political bodies rather than military bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are the practical activities of crisis staffs? Don't give us many definitions. How do they prepare for the aggression of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The basic task of the crisis staffs was as follows: To ensure equipment and armament, to organise defence, and to establish frontlines towards the army of Republika Srpska, to accept displaced persons, to give shelter from air attacks to the population, and to take over the barracks of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now tell me, in what way was this army gathering or these armed people? Was there mobilisation or was it done in a different way?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: At that time, neither the organisational conditions, nor the personnel, was such as to allow a mobilisation to be carried out. What was made were lists of volunteers in villages that would be ready to take weapons in their arms and go to the front with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, would that mean that volunteers would come to a particular place in a village or a town and basically say, "I'm ready to go to war"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: That was precisely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me how units were formed? Were they mobile units that were formed or were units formed on a territorial basis?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: At that time, when crisis staffs were being formed, lists -- and I stress there were lists -- this is still far away from a real organisation of units, so the lists of volunteers were carried out according to their place of residence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would a unit be formed in the village where they lived?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: In those villages, out of the lists of volunteers, people who had responsibilities, those people were, by the way, also on those lists, they would use, in their organisations, the names such as "platoon" or "company" or some other usual term known in the military organisation. But what is important to stress here is that those terms would not result from their norms of organisation, but it was the way in which the commander of a particular village would see this organisation. For example, we had a village with some 40 soldiers, and those villages would call it a company. Another village would have 100 soldiers and they would also call it a company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that these executives in the crisis staff and the leaders in villages, they would use military terms, but, in fact, every village was a military unit, regardless of its name?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the situation alike with Croats and with Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: What I've just mentioned for the HVO, at that time, the same goes for the Muslims as well. That means that in the local commune, in the village, they had a unit just as I've described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you mean to say, one village means one military unit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: That is correct. Let me try and clarify the term "village" and try to present the situation that we had there at that time. I must stress one fact, and that is, what was a village in Bosnia that was preparing for the war? It was a logistics base. It was a base for receiving new personnel. And if that village was at an important location, for example, on an important road, during the war, it was very often a military stronghold which was defending itself and where there were battles. I've got a schematic that may show, in the easiest possible way, what the first lists of volunteers looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could we have the computer monitor switched on, please? Also, could you dim the lights, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, what can we see on this map?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: On this map, first of all, the scale is 1:50.000, which you can see on the legend. What does that mean? It means that 1 centimetre on this map represents 500 metres in nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I don't think we can see it on the monitors, as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Small technical problems. Until we clarify those -- yes, we have the map now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let's try and see what we have got here. There are three colours here, blue, green, red, and some circles. What does that mean? What were your intentions?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: In blue are villages or towns where the units of the HVO are being organised, and in green are units which are being organised by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us in which municipalities?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: This map represents the area of responsibility of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which municipalities?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: We can easily see that here are the municipalities of Vitez, Busovaca, Novi Travnik, Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In blue, can you repeat what you said?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The villages where HVO units were being organised, and in green are shown villages where BH army units are being organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this correspond with the fact that where the HVO is being organised, the majority of the village or municipality is Croatian, and where the BH army is being organised, the majority is Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to you, this was the structure of units, the deployment of both people?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. That is their deployment on the 24th of April, 1992 up until June 1993. There is another thing that I would like to stress regarding this map. We can see that in red, there are lines and the forces of Republika Srpska. And especially because of this time period, this is already in April 1992, I want to point out this blue line that is next to the red line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are going to speak about that later, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: But I would, nevertheless, like to mention that already at that time, the HVO, with the units that it had, had a front-line with the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now go back to the crisis staff. You said that its main feature was the volunteers, people come and become volunteers. Another characteristic was that one village was one unit. Can you tell us how the commanders were selected? Those people who were at the head of these units, how was it structured?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Commanders in the villages were chosen by the locals themselves. As for the commanders at the level of the municipality, those were appointed with the approval of political representatives of the village. That is the people who would head the crisis staff and the units at the level of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, the military commanders were not appointed from the top down, as is customary in the army, but through democratic elections in the municipality or the village?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. As a result, the chain of command at the beginning was not fully respected because, Counsel, as you mentioned yourself, this was based on voluntariness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about the next characteristic which I consider to be important for understanding the army of the HVO and the BH army, at least at the beginning, that is logistics. How did these people from August '91 until April '92, until the beginning of the war when barracks were captured by the HVO and the TO jointly, and distributed in Central Bosnia; up to that point in time, up to April, how did people supply themselves with arms?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: There were several sources. One which was widely used was that people would purchase weapons with their own funds, as well as other equipment for the purpose of defence. Another way was by capturing barracks in the Lasva River Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to that later.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: These were barracks within the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia, and then through certain companies, through the municipal bodies; in fact, non-regular forms of supply, each and every one found a way to obtain weapons to defend himself, a rifle or a piece of clothing that would give him the status of a soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, we have described the crisis staffs which were dominant until about April 1992 and which were formed in the municipalities. Tell me, in that period, in Central Bosnia, were regional staffs formed as well? Was there a higher level of organisation above the municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. In that time period, because of the seriousness of the situation along the front with the Army of Republika Srpska and the need to coordinate activities, a regional staff, or rather a regional crisis staff was set up whose role was to coordinate activities among several municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it composed also of politicians rather than soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us proceed. We come to May 1992, and the crisis staffs are renamed to municipal HVO staffs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did that mean? What really changed with this change of name?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the crisis staffs changed their method of organisation at the end of April 1992. The assignments of the crisis staffs, or rather of the municipal staffs, were identical with those of the crisis staffs. However, what were the substantive differences? The municipal staffs were structured in such a way that, in addition to the commander, there were assistants and chiefs of staff. Consequently, these municipal staffs were more of a military body than the crisis staffs, because we had specific appointments; the chief of engineers, the chief of staffs and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, it is a step forward towards a military mode of organisation in relation to the previous stage?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to these municipal staffs, in the chain of command, there was also a regional staff which had a command coordinating function.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before we move on, I should like to ask the usher to help me with this document. And I should like to ask you, Brigadier, to look at it and tell us what it represents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just want a point of clarification. The regional staff replaced the village staffs, or were there two at the same time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, at the lower level of organisation, at the level of the local commune, a crisis staff remained. At the level of the municipality there was also a crisis staff. The regional staff was above the municipal staff with a coordinating function. And it was established in response to the need to coordinate the forces in the villages that we have been speaking about and to provide better quality engagement of those units along the front-line of the Army of Republika Srpska. After this period, that is the end of April 1992, the crisis staffs were renamed to become municipal staffs. In local communities, units remained, the platoons and the companies, in the villages, as up until then; but at the level above the municipality, a regional staff or headquarters was established. The difference between crisis staffs and municipal staffs was in their composition. The crisis staffs were composed of political representatives, and the municipal staffs had their commanders and were composed of military officers, assistants and chiefs for various branches and specialties of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So, you're talking about the municipal staffs, so that became military bodies, and it dominated others, this staff, it was the command.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the municipal staff was the highest form of command at the level of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D199, D199A for the English and D199B for the French.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we look at it on the ELMO? Tell me, please, is this a document dated 10th of May, 1992, where the municipal staff from Kiseljak says, in the first item, "The crisis staff is renamed to become the municipal staff of the HVO," signed Tihomir Blaskic? Do you recognise the signature, first?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I do. This is the signature of General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this one of the documents reflecting the change of name and organisational structures you have just explained?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. From this document we can see the organisational changes that I have described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, in that period of time, the regional headquarters, the regional staff, did it have a superior command position that was automatically implemented at the level of the municipalities? Or did it coordinate the work of the municipalities on the basis of a political agreement rather than a military order? What was the relationship between the regional commands and the municipal commands?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The regional command at the time had more of a coordinating function in relation to the municipal commands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, there wasn't a clear chain of command?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, when these municipal commands were formed at the end of April, beginning of May 1992, which were the problems that emerged in that period in the functioning of the municipal commands and their work on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, at the time the municipal commands were being established there were a variety of problems, and on this occasion I should like to refer to only a few. First of all, the entire organisation was based on voluntariness, which made difficult the functioning of the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us stop there. You said that this voluntary principle made it difficult, but when we look at films we consider volunteers to be the greatest, the most, the bravest combatants in the world. Do you consider voluntariness to be a bad thing for an army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I think it has its disadvantages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Voluntariness, in simple terms, implies that a soldier or a conscript applies on a voluntary basis to join. But similarly, he is free to leave a certain organisation, because you have no instrument, when he is a volunteer, to fit him within the structure because of the overall situation in which you are working and living.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said he goes to the front voluntarily and he can also go back when he likes. Could he be simply moved from his own village 50 kilometres away, if he is a volunteer in his own village and the surroundings? Is he also a volunteer for going 50 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: That is precisely the problem. Voluntariness, in the conditions that were prevalent at the time, meant that people were ready to defend their homes and nothing more than that. And in the deployment of armed forces, according to military standards, the army must be deployed wherever the need arises. In those cases this voluntariness was a problem for us. May I refer briefly to the situation we had at the time? That is why I stressed the existence of the defence line facing the Army of Republika Srpska. The situation was as follows, and I shall try and demonstrate this problem of voluntariness, and there were many more. By way of an example, you need to engage 100 men for the defence line facing the Army of Republika Srpska, from the level of the regional command, you issue an order to the municipal commands, shall we say to Travnik, Novi Travnik, Kiseljak or Vitez, to somebody you are sure will carry out that order one hundred per cent. Probably he will be the one whose house is very close to the defence line. But if a soldier has to cover 20 or 30 kilometres in order to defend another village, then the execution of that order may be called in question. That is the substance of the problem of voluntariness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Brigadier, this period of April or May '92 and onwards; was this the period when the Army of Republika Srpska was bringing ever stronger pressure to bear, especially in the area of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: At the time the pressure on the defence lines held by the HVO were becoming more and more intensified, especially in the area of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, was there a strong wave of displaced persons coming from areas from which the Army of Republika Srpska had expelled them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: That problem in the area of Central Bosnia, and particularly in the Lasva River Valley, was a major one, this phenomenon, I would call it. And in the first place, the number of displaced persons was very large, both of Croats and Muslim Bosniaks. But in this same period of time, what happened was that Croatian refugees went to Herzegovina, Croatia and to other countries; whereas the displaced Muslims or Bosniaks remained within the territory of Central Bosnia. They stayed on in the Lasva River Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you use the term displaced persons, are you referring only to women, children and the elderly, or also soldiers or civilians that were under arms among both peoples?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: All those who were familiar with developments and the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina must know that the structure of displaced persons was such that all age groups were represented; children, women, elderly, conscripts, able-bodied men, the entire population from a particular region from which they had been expelled. But I should also like to mention that this number of displaced persons, both Bosniaks and Croats, was coming from the area of north-western Bosnia, from the municipalities of Prijedor, Donja Luka, Sanski Most, Bosanski Petrovac, Kljuc, Donji Vakuf, Kotor Varos, and other places and towns which were situated in north-western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, there was ethnic cleansing in those areas and all these people were concentrated in Central Bosnia. Did this aggravate the security situation with this river of displaced persons arriving?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Such a large influx of people, and especially after Jajce fell, aggravated the security situation in the area of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia and in the area of the Lasva Valley. At the time a problem that arose were frequent disturbances of public law and order. There were thefts of vehicles, the setting up of checkpoints which were not under anyone's control, and similar incidents which affected the security situation in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Brigadier, these disturbances of the public law and order, this deterioration of safety and threats to people and property; was this directed against a single ethnic group or the whole population?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: It affected everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened with the civilian bodies of authority inherited from the former Yugoslavia, the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? I'm primarily referring to the civilian police, the judiciary, the Prosecutor's office; how did these bodies function under these aggravated circumstances in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The developments that I have referred to in the course of my presentation affected the functioning of civilian authorities adversely. But one of the main reasons for the failure of these civilian authorities to function, in my opinion, is linked to the inadequate functioning of the central authorities in Sarajevo. But, what it is particularly important to underline, when observing or analysing the security situation in the area, is the functioning of the civilian police. The civilian police, inherited from the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the circumstances that were prevalent in the area, did not have the necessary credibility among the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: In order to be able to perform its police duties. In my view the reasons are twofold. On the one hand you have combatants, people under arms who are defending and holding the lines along the front against the Army of Republika Srpska. And these men, and all others who did not have such a role, had gained possession of weapons which was more effective than the weapons of the police. So, the equipment of the police undermined the quality of their policing. Furthermore, this situation was immediately recognised by criminal groups who started forming bands and gangs to achieve their criminal intents. And in those circumstances the police, such as it was with the equipment it had, with the personnel, inherited from an institution that no longer existed, could hardly perform the tasks it was meant to perform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now, Brigadier, move on to the formation of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia and the operative groups. We can now go on to the next map. We will be reviewing a number of documents. Will you tell us how the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia was formed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: To the backdrop of the problems that I have referred to here, and with the aim of overcoming the consequences which were evident, steps were taken to reorganise the existing structure so that as of November, 1992, the municipal commands were abolished and brigades were established. The regional commands are abolished or rather transformed into an Operational Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Talking about operative zones, could the usher please hand out this document so that we can see the structure of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked 200, 200A for the French version, and 200B for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is D200. Please, Brigadier, look at the Croatian version, please. First of all, let us identify this document dated the 7th of October, 1992. Has it been initialled by the then Colonel Blaskic, or is it somebody else's initial?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: This was initialled by Colonel Mijo Bozic, who signed the document on behalf of General Blaskic, and he was authorised to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you tell us here, we have mentioned the organisational transformation from one form into the other, of course an Operational Zone, operational groups; can you tell us what an Operational Zone is and what is an operational group? What comes above the other form?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, when it comes to Operational Zones, we have to bear in mind that that is the command which was superior to the then municipal commands for those municipalities that were on the territory for which the command of the Operational Zone was responsible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now read out to whom this document was addressed. Could you tell the Judges, after that; was the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia with Blaskic at its head?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, please, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I asked Mr. Dubuisson to put every document on the ELMO for the assistance of the translators, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please, Mr. Dubuisson.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's already been done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm now going to read you which municipalities Blaskic is sending this order: Kresevo, Kiseljak, Sarajevo, Fonjica, Vares, Kakanj, Busovaca, Vitez, Travnik, Novi Travnik, Zenica, Maglaj, Teslic and Tesanj. All these municipalities, were they parts of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As well as Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what an operational group is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Depending on the situation that was on the front-line towards Republika Srpska, and in order to organise the defences more efficiently within the command of the Operational Zone, operative groups were established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: In order to coordinate and prepare and perform defence activities in a better way, and also because of the large territory that was given to the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, do you mean to say that the territory under the control of Colonel Blaskic was so large that already at that time it was not possible to command it efficiently from one headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't mind the long speeches by Mr. Nobilo, but I think it would better serve the Court and everybody if Mr. Nobilo would ask a question and allow the Brigadier to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you have been carried away too much and you have gone slightly over and beyond what your duties were. This is your witness. Please ask him questions and then wait for his answers. You cannot make commentaries. These are commentaries made before the question. You can't make that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm trying to be efficient in my work. I'm trying to summarise the answer so that we should not lose too much time by a series of small questions, but I can adapt to your wishes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, was it possible to govern, efficiently, such a large operational zone?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Precisely, because that was not possible. Operational groups were established. The commanders of operational groups were commanders from the most important brigade in the area where an operational group was formed. I used the term "brigade" but brigades were being established at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you tell us, for the record, and for the Judges, what were the operational groups in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, and what was their territory?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, in the territory and in the area of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia, three operational groups were formed. The first operational group were the municipalities, that is, the municipal commands of Travnik, Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, and Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. I did not understand what the first one was.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Travnik, Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. On the document, I probably made a mistake whilst reading. I thought the first one was the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You've read it well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, have you got the document? According to this document, what happened later on and what was later on restructured? You will explain that later on, but according to this document, how were the organisational groups organised?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: According to this document and its time period, it is dated the 7th of October, 1992, we can see, and that is how things really were, that four operational groups had been formed. I've already gone one step further. Excuse me for that. So there were four operational groups, and the composition of those operational groups was as follows: The municipalities of Travnik, Novi Travnik, Vitez, Jajce, and Zenica were renamed to become the 1st Operational Group. The municipalities of Kiseljak, Kresevo, Busovaca, Fojnica, Vares, Kakanj, and Sarajevo, the 3rd Operational Zone became part of the 2nd Operational Group. The municipalities of Zepce, Zavidovici, Maglaj, Teslic and Tesanj became part of the 3rd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you tell the Judges whether, later on, some changes were made and whether some municipalities moved to become parts of different operational groups?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. That did happen, and that is why I answered previously as I did. I would like to apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Busovaca, which operational group was it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: After the transformation of the already established operational groups, the municipality of Busovaca became part of the 1st Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now pass on to the command of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher to help us distribute a document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document D201 and D201A for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, please take a look at this document dated the 18th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, it's almost 11.20 now. As we are now moving into important issues of command, the witness will have time to look at the document closely, and we can meet again in twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please have the accused brought in. I apologise for the delay. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You must know that when we resume with delay, it means that when Judges are having a break, they have to deal with papers, telephone calls, and various other matters, so that we don't always manage to come on time. As I criticise the parties when they are late, I have to present our excuses, the only consolation being that it gives the interpreters more time to recuperate because we're asking them to work rather longer hours than would be normal. We are going to talk about document D200 now, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you look at this document? It is dated the 18th of November, 1992, and let us first see the signature. Do you recognise the signature of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does this document represent? Will you please explain to the Court?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this document was drafted in the command of the Operative Zone. It represents the desired structure of the command of the Operative Zone, what the commander of the Operative Zone wanted to have in his command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, what did Colonel Blaskic think at the time? How many men did he need to be able to control the Operative Zone that we have described? How many men did he need in the command?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: According to this document and the ideas of the commander of the Operative Zone, his assessment was that, in order to execute their tasks, they would need roughly 105 to 106 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have some experience now in the Federation Army. You are regularly in touch with NATO experts. What are the NATO standards for the command of an operative zone of this size? How many officers and non-commissioned officers would be required in the command of an operative zone, according to NATO standards?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: As far as I know, for this level of command, one that is comparable to the Operative Zone, the number would be 220 to 225 personnel, persons in the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell Their Honours, please, how many of you were there in the command of the Operative Zone at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: At the time this document was drafted, and in the drafting of which I personally participated, there were about 20, 23 -- 23 to 25 of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Out of those 23 or 25 men, instead of the 100 that Blaskic had wanted and the 220 envisaged by NATO standards, how many officers were there who were graduates of military academies and with military experience?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: At the time, we had three officers who were graduates of the military academy, but not with any considerable military experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us the names of those three officers in the command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: There was General Blaskic, Brigadier Ivica Zeko, and Colonel Mijo Bozic who were graduates of the military academy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ranks you mentioned are current ranks and not the ranks they held at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain to the Court, you now have an Operative Zone formed; you have a military command formed. Were the problems that you mentioned earlier, from voluntariness to the principle one village, one unit that you were confronted with in the previous period, overcome?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The command of the Operative Zone, composed in this way, was the result of continuous efforts on the part of the commander of the Operative Zone to militarise the organisation and the soldiers under his command. However, in view of the problems that I mentioned before, and let me repeat them again, they were the principle of voluntary participation in armed forces, the inadequate functioning of the chain of command, the strong pressure of the army of Republika Srpska on our defence lines, the large number of refugees, and disturbances of public law and order, the situation did not change much. We did have the organisation we wanted set up, but the situation on the ground did not change much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will come back to the chain of command later, but tell us now, were there any combat forces prepared, in combat readiness?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Combat-ready forces in the territory of Central Bosnia did not exist. Combat-ready forces means personnel in one place in a barracks which have their duties, which are undergoing training, who are adequately equipped, who have the necessary officers and non-commissioned officers who prepare the personnel and who organise those combat forces. We did not have such forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Instead of that, what did you have? What did your army look like?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: As we said at the beginning, the organisation of the HVO was carried out by enlisting men from the villages, and this was the method applied virtually throughout the war. We have already said what the problems were, which means that we still had men living in their own homes. They had weapons. When the need arose to go to the defence lines against the army of Republika Srpska, then a list would be made, a commander appointed, and then this group -- if it numbered some 30 men, it would be called a platoon; if it was 50 or more, it would be called a company -- and this group would go to carry out its assignment, to defend the lines for seven to ten days continuously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you had a group of people, determined the commanders, and they would be sent to the front. They would be the army. What would happen to those men when they were not on the defence lines, when they were in their villages? What was their status then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: After carrying out their task on the defence lines, for a period of seven to ten days, those men would return to their homes and to their regular duties. Some of them went to work in their companies, others worked at home, and others still travelled, depending on their family obligations. It is very important to point out that when the soldiers returned from the defence lines and went home, then it was simply not possible to have command over them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, were they then civilians?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: They were civilians, and that was their status.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that they performed their regular duties in their companies. Are these civilian companies and civilian affairs?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. These were civilian duties and civilian companies because, as I said, men from all the companies existing within a certain village would go to the front, which means a teacher, a locksmith, or anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When a person came back from the defence line, would he have to hand back his uniform?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Each soldier would take his uniform and his weapon home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he didn't go to the defence line, what was the custom? Did those young men like to wear their uniforms or did they prefer civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: To make my answer clearer, we have to go back to the situation as it was at the time. To wear a uniform, at the time, was an indication of pride. It was an indication that one was a defender. It meant popularity. So that after completing their assignments on the front, they would go home, and if they felt like it, the next day, they would go to town, to cafes, wearing those uniforms, because they wanted to be seen by their neighbours as soldiers, because they took pride in that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let me ask for the usher's assistance now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document 202 and 202A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have a French version, don't you, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson is used to not having a French version, so he forgot to mention it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There was a French version, but it was hidden in the pile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, will you have a look at these tables, please, and tell us what they represent?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: From this list, we can see the way in which soldiers were engaged for the defence line. We can see that for those activities, they were remunerated, depending on the number of days they spent on the front-line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, we can see on the first two pages that they all had the same salary in one month, whereas on the following pages, each individual had a different salary. How do you explain this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: From this list, we can also see that the persons on the first page are commanders and members of the command who were working in the command. On list number 3, marked as page 1, at least in my copy, one can see that the soldiers have a different number of days. This confirms the way in which men were engaged for the defence line facing the army of Republika Srpska, and, partly, too, it explains how they were remunerated for these assignments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, after the column with the names, then we have the duty, then basic salary, then the number of days. Don't we see, in this column, how many days each individual spent as a soldier during that month? Can that clearly be seen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. That can clearly be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this date back to the time when we had municipal commands?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: From the stamp, this is an example from the municipality of Kresevo. There were similar such documents from the other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now say a few words about the strength of the individual units. Can you confirm, on the basis of the stamp and the contents, that this is an authentic list of salaries, that is, document D202?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. I can confirm that this was a document drafted in the municipal command of Kresevo.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is document D203, which has no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, there must be a mistake. We will introduce this document this afternoon or tomorrow, because, due to the large number of documents, we are unable to find the translation for the moment. So we can proceed to another document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, will you tell us, by way of conclusion, what would you say was typical of the structure in 1992, briefly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: As a conclusion regarding the HVO structure at the time, I should like to point out the following: The organisation was based on voluntariness which caused problems in the functioning of the chain of command. There was no responsibility. Furthermore, the shortage of qualified personnel with military training and experience; also, the method of appointing and dismissing commanders. What does that mean? A major influence and a decisive role was played by the municipal functionaries, if we are talking about commanders at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "municipal functionaries," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I'm referring to politicians at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: When we're talking about the municipality, as for lower level units, the decisive role was played by the villages themselves or, rather, the villagers. Another problem that I would like to underline or, rather, another conclusion, there were no regulations regarding the structure, which means that units were formed on a territorial principle which had, as a consequence, that there were relationships of familiarity among members, rather than relations of subordination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean when you talk about this familiarity relationship? Could you explain how that worked in practice?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: In practice, it worked as follows: A soldier that would commit an error or a mistake would be disciplined. For example, because of his links, family links with somebody else in the same unit, because they would come from the same village, the result would be that the local commander would try to hide it away and the real commander would never learn of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This local commander, would he care more for the opinion of his commander or of his unit that appointed him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: A commander in the village was caring more about the opinions of the members of his unit and of other villages who were not soldiers. Only after that, then he would take into account the carrying out of the mission that he received from his superior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: There were no real facilities and ways in holding older people together; so, the people would go to the front-line and come back. It was very difficult, because of the lack of proper facilities, to build proper military discipline. Furthermore, what I think was important is when an army is established in the situation of war, what does it mean? You saw the document about structure of the commander, that is what a commander really wished for. But the real situation in the field, in the units, was different and more difficult, which means that a commander of the Operative Zone had in front of him, as a project, the creation of a command structure. That was what his intentions were, that was what he strived for, and General Blaskic worked diligently on that. But, the real situation in the field was difficult with all the problems that I've mentioned up to now. Also, the logistic supplies and the way it was done also had an influence on the structure and the functioning in the HVO units. What impact did it have? The logistics supplies were ensured individually, which meant that you would, yourself, buy a uniform or your weapon. Who would then be able to take it away from you? Because you are the only owner of it, and you decide how to use it. Also, some companies helped to achieve supplying with weapons and uniforms, and we said that they were linked with the municipal authorities. All that had an impact on the organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, isn't there a saying in Bosnia that says you obey the one who feeds you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, that was true in our case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you speak about companies, do you mean state-owned companies and private companies?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: There were private companies, but there were also individuals that worked in state-owned companies that had the possibilities through exchange of goods. For example, somebody who was able to buy some weapons headed that towards a company, and that is the way it was done. But in that case, that company would automatically have some influence on that particular unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there something else you would like to say?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Something else that I would like to point out was the way the units were organised on the defence lines. Let me remind you of what I already said. I've said that on the defence lines soldiers were engaged according to our needs here. You've got the defence lines, these were the defence lines towards the Army of Republika Srpska in the time period I'm talking of, so, we had a need to send 50 soldiers there. How are we going to do that? We're going to make a list of those people, and then for that particular task we will appoint a commander. So, there wouldn't be a permanent commander who would go there, but those men would go to the defence lines and carry out the tasks, and during that time they act more or less within a military structure; but later on they would come back and go home. That represented a problem for us for having a proper ensuring of defence lines and their proper quality. Because, when you haven't got permanent soldiers, then you do not know how to organise yourself well, because the enemy can strike when you're not well organised. In order to try and avoid that, we had difficulties because we might not be having enough soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it have an influence on how to control the behaviour of soldiers when they were not on the defence lines?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, because once they would go back home they were free and they could, they started, first of all, to go into town dressed in uniforms, and later they started going to towns under arms, and there were problems in the law and order. They created disorders. I, under the order and instruction of General Blaskic, wrote orders trying to normalise the situation and improve the security of the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, now we are coming to an issue which I think will be important, and I think it is important for the Judges to hear it, and that is, the topic of security in the area of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. What were the most common ways in which crimes were perpetrated or how much disorder was created?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: In the time period we are talking of I would like to point out the following: The voluntary use of weapons without any control, the start of shooting, that means. Then there were checkpoints that would appear. Then vehicles would be stolen. Let me give you a personal example. I was born in Novi Travnik and that is where I lived. I had, even before the war, a certain social place. I was chief of the operational department. But the situation was such that I had a car, as I worked in the command post in Vitez. For security reasons I put that car with my parents in a village, because I was not sure that two or three days upon my return home I would find the vehicle again. Another personal example, when there was a large number of displaced persons and refugees that had arrived, I was to ensure my apartment. If I would go away for two or three days, what happened, somebody broke in to my apartment. Although people knew who I was, but the criminals would not choose their targets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they move into your apartment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, they did; and I had to clarify the situation myself, and I managed to solve it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us these savage checkpoints, what did they represent in Central Bosnia at that time? Who founded them and why?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: When we speak about these savage checkpoints, we obviously think that there must have been some regular checkpoints, there were legal checkpoints, yes; first of all, for the control and for an improvement of the security situation. When we speak about these savage checkpoints, or random checkpoints, these were done by individuals who put them out because they had arms at home, they were well armed, so the police could not face them; and their purpose was plundering and theft. They thought that they might take something away in such a manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would such a theft at a random checkpoint, was it mono-ethnic? For example, if Croats had a checkpoint, would they try and steal from Muslims, or would they steal regardless of the nationality?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Regardless of the nationality. For example, you had a checkpoint in a Croatian village, and then they would have a deal and establish with others in a checkpoint in a Muslim village, and they made deals and they stole whatever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When criminal groups appeared, why couldn't the police do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: As time went by, the security situation got worse from day to day. Criminals would manage to reach their goals, and these criminal groups then became stronger and stronger. They were better armed than the police, and the police lacked credibility that it needed, and lacked equipment. And so, in that situation they were not able to undertake anything appropriate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you're speaking about various equipment, could you tell us very concretely what weapons had the criminal groups and what weapons had the police?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The criminal groups had, we can say, all infantry weapons. They had automatic weapons, they had machine guns, they even had some rocket launchers; whereas the police, if they had something, had rifles, most often they had pistols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the civilian police there was also military police; what was the basic problem for the selection of the military police so that it could not replace the civilian police, which was not efficient, in order to prevent criminal deeds?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The military police was also established without any rules and regulations. Also, the members of the military police became so, on a voluntary basis. There were no criteria established for someone to become a member of the military police. So, there were situations where members of the military police would become people who had criminal tendencies, and also people who lacked qualifications for carrying out the duties of military police, and those were people who lacked basic education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Brigadier, in this whole area of the Lasva River Valley, was there any forensic centre? Was there any centre for legal medicine and so on?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: No, no, that did not exist, neither at the time nor today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher to help us with a new document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is the document D204, D204A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, in order not to read the whole document, and also for the audiences that are here who do not know what it is all about, I would prefer to read some more important parts of this document and so that they would be in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm astonished that the public can't have access to them, because I think they can be put on the ELMO. If the document is on the ELMO --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it can be seen on the screen, in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You can see it now. If this is a public session, I think that the public can see the document. That seems obvious to me, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, the second brigade, this is a group, and I will read it to you. "Report on the activities of groups and individuals acting without the knowledge of the HVO." I'm only reading the first paragraph and then I will have some questions to put to you. "Groups and individuals looting, socially and more often privately owned property are causing serious problems in the Vitez municipality. During the robberies they make use of all forms of standard crime. Their main objective is to loot. However, as nobody is making an effort to put end to this, their criminal offences put an additional strain on the already tense inter-ethnic relations. Lately, local robbers have been cooperating with soldiers from Herzegovina in the looting of privately owned property who have become emboldened and Herzegovins have been trying to loot privately owned buildings by themselves." I now draw your attention to the last sentence of the front page: "Life and international relations have reached a critical point due to these numerous robberies, break-ins and explosions. There haven't been many casualties but we must energetically oppose these occurrences. We have reached a point where large scale action is necessary, which will be enthusiastically welcomed by the inhabitants of Vitez municipality, regardless of nationality, and which will finally restore the honour and reputation of the uniform we all wear. Administrative assistant for SIS, Security and Information Service, Ivan Budimir. Brigadier, do you remember this report and these deeds and Ivan Budimir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I know Mr. Budimir. I also know the typist. It is Madam Nada Budza. I remember also these events, and the situation was such as it is described in this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The text speaks for itself. So, if you have confirmed that the situation was actually such, I have no questions about it anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we now have the next document, please? Has the previous document been marked? I don't think we have got a number. Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The previous document was D204 and D204A for the English translation. Now we have got document D205, D205A for the French version and D205B for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, here we have got a document D205 dated 22nd of January, 1993, and written by the same person, Ivan Budimir, who was mentioned in the previous document. This is a report about throwing of explosive devices in the town, and in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Brigade. On the 22nd of January, 1993, as the report says, an explosive device was thrown in front of the Red Cross, and the kebab shop, and in front of the ambulance and the civilian police, and also in front of the building called Crnogorka. It also says that somebody used a hand-held rocket launcher to hit the apartment of Zoran Krizanovic. So, tell me, now, do you recall these events and is this just an example of many such cases?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I remember the event quite well. This was the most conspicuous example of the situation that prevailed in the area and of the fact that all kinds of devices were used, as in this case. The aim being to disturb the public law and order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us in which town this happened?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: This happened in the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us try, for the needs of this case -- we must look at things from the ethnic standpoint. Who was the damaged party? Zoran Krizanovic, whose apartment was hit by some kind of a hand-held rocket launcher, what ethnic group does he belong to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under whose control was the civilian police on the 22nd of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: On the 22nd of January, 1993, the policemen -- let me just recall, the MUP was composed of Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the health clinic in January, under whose control was it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The employees were Croats and the patients were also partly Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Red Cross, whose institution was that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: This particular Red Cross building, that is, at the one operating at the level of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who held power in Vitez municipality at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Croats held the executive power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Crnogorka building, is it a large apartment building where representatives of all three ethnic groups lived?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. Within that block called Crnogorka, there was a part that was still under construction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: May I ask the usher for his assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document D206, D206A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, I will, again, be referring to certain parts of this document. Let me first ask you, it is a document signed by Ivan Budimir and Nada Budza on the 13th of January, 1993 in the 2nd Battalion in Vitez. Do you recognise those signatures?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read points 1, 2, and 3 of this report, which is headed "Report on Security in the 2nd Vitez Battalion." "1) Over the last week, Muslims have been reporting to us on a daily basis with a desire to join our units. There have been, altogether, five such cases so far, and there are indications that there will be more. 2) The newly arrived HVO units from Herzegovina are causing us great difficulties. Every evening, they walk around the town with weapons and disturb the citizens by firing bursts of fire while intoxicated. This problem is all the more serious because of the school classes that are going on in Vitez, which means there are many children on the streets. We are afraid that an even more serious incident could occur. There was an attempt to take a car from our chief of communications, Zoran Jukic. 3) A drunken BH army soldier was sighted in the zone protected and monitored by our units in the area of Kuber. The problem was resolved, but a warning was sent to the BH army stating our intention to respond with fire to any similar incidents in the future, because all this occurred around 2.30 hours in the morning." Does this report correspond to the real state of affairs at the time in the town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: May I ask the usher for his assistance with the next document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D207, D207A for the French version, and D207B for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, do you have a copy?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just read a couple of points, and then we can ask you about your memories of this problem. It is the Command of the Vitez Brigade dated the 8th of April, 1993. The heading is "Ban on the Movement of Uniformed Individuals and the Bearing of Arms in Inhabited Areas." Then we have the preamble to the order: "Due to frequent disturbances of public peace and order, murders, wounding, armed threats, firing at inhabited areas, and the deterioration in the security situation in general, and pursuant to the order of Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, I hereby order: 1) Uniformed individuals are banned from bearing arms and wearing uniforms in all inhabited areas and roads when military personnel are not on duty, except during travel to and from the frontlines." I will leave out a couple of points, even though they are all important, but to speed up the proceedings. "4) Small arms (pistols, revolvers, etc.) may be borne with the appropriate permit only. Long-barrelled weapons may be borne by military and civilian policeman only. 6) Any person who opens fire at inhabited areas without permission shall be promptly disarmed, regardless of permission and reported to the appropriate commander," signed "Brigade Commander, Mario Cerkez." Tell me, Brigadier, do you recognise Mario Cerkez's signature, and do you recognise Blaskic's order, which was the basis for this order by Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I do. This is Mario Cerkez's signature, and General Blaskic did, indeed, issue an order, on the basis of which the brigade commander issued his own order for his unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Briefly, what was the immediate cause prompting Blaskic to order his subordinates to ban movement of men in uniform and bearing long barrels?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I shall remind you of what I said, briefly. The fact that soldiers returning from the front-line went home in uniform and bearing weapons, and in doing so, they disturbed the public law and order. There were criminal groups and other such incidents which jeopardised the safety of people in the area. So the need arose, within the chain of command, to issue such an order to improve the situation and to improve security, so that it would be acceptable for the inhabitants of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher for his assistance with the next document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document D208, D208A for the French version, D208B for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, it is a brief order, and I will read it. On 6th of February, 1993, the commander, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, sends to all HVO brigades and independent zones in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia: "Warning, for failure to carry out the command number 01-1-217/93 of 10 January, 1993," and then the warning says: "By the command number 01-1-217/93 dated 10 January, 1993, and in connection with repeated occurrences of the disturbance of public law and order, murders, injuries, threats with firearms, opening fire in inhabited places, as well as a worsening of the overall security situation, concrete duties have been established to combat such negative acts and proceedings. Until today, adequate and efficient measures have not been taken, that the aforesaid negative tendencies have been vented, to a larger extent, I warn all commanders of brigades and independent units in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia of their duty to carry out the aforesaid commands. The measures and actions taken pursuant to this command should be reported to this command headquarters by 8th February, 1993," signed "Commander Colonel Tihomir Blaskic." Brigadier, are you familiar with this order?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: This is a warning that I personally wrote, which can be seen from my initials in the left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us clear this up immediately. How does one know who actually wrote an order when it was not written by the commander?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: In order that it be known who wrote a document, and in order to monitor its operative implementation, we established the rule, and I believe such a rule was applied in the former army, that in the left-hand corner of the document, the initials should be placed of the author of the text and, secondly, the initials of the typist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when we see "SM," that means that it was you who actually wrote the document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was it necessary for Blaskic to repeat the same thing twice, sometimes more, as we will see later on?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: This warning and its contents is evidence of the seriousness of the situation regarding public law and order within the territory of Central Bosnia and, particularly, in the Lasva Valley.
