If an order was issued, as it was, the one whose number is mentioned in the preamble dated the 18th of January, 1993, by monitoring its implementation, we have established that it was not being implemented, in fact, that the situation was worsening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the reason that low-level units cannot or will not carry out orders? What is the cause?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The cause of such a situation was what I have already mentioned when talking about the characteristics of the organisation. The reasons were, therefore, familiarity, the voluntary principle, the lack of qualified military personnel and experienced military personnel, and also the absence of instruments to deal with crime, because you didn't have the necessary resources in order to restore law and order and place the situation fully under control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, you have obviously written some or most of the orders. Could you tell us, what was the position of Colonel Blaskic? Did he tolerate violence on the part of HVO soldiers towards Muslims and prohibit violence by HVO soldiers towards Croats, or did he have a uniform position, that the victim of violence is always a victim?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Will you put your question directly, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Colonel Blaskic's position regarding crime? Would he tolerate crime at the expense of Vitez citizens of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: General Blaskic never allowed it. For him, crime was crime, and he used all available forces and resources to combat all forms of crime, regardless of who the targets were. This can be seen from these two documents and, I believe, from other documents as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can I call on the usher for his assistance, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D209, D209A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, I'll be reading parts of this report compiled on the 16th of March, 1993 by the Vitez Brigade and the officer on duty, Ivan Budimir. The report is on the 15th and 16th of March, 1993, so I'm reading the text now: "At 1810 hours on the 15th of March, 1993, a loud explosion was heard from the centre of town. The MUP, "that is, the police," and the OIO Centre were informed about it. It was later established that an explosive device or a bomb had been thrown in front of the Maks store where there were many passers-by, of whom several were slightly injured. A few cars parked in the parking lot were also damaged." I'm going on to the next paragraph of this report. "On the 15th of March, 1993, at 1915 hours, Ivica Drnic, a company commander, informed us that a group of Muslims were intercepting, stopping, and searching people travelling to Veceriska." I will leave out two lines. Then it says: "We have learned that Ferhet Haskic was the leader of the group in question. The BiH Army Command (Zikret Ahmic) was informed about this, and their representatives immediately went to the scene of the incident to intervene along with military policemen." I leave out two lines, and then I'm reading: "We were informed that the military police of the BH Army would take Ferhet Haskic into custody on the 16th of March, 1993."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see the name "Ferhet Haskic," and above it says "Fikret."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The name is "Ferhet." In my Croatian text, it is "Ferhet Haskic," and Zikret is the military policeman who received the report and who went to intervene against Haskic. Zikret Ahmic is from the BH army command to whom the Croats complained, and then he intervened against Haskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next paragraph, on the 16th of March, 1993, at 0055 hours, according to company commander Ivica Drnic, "An explosive device was thrown in front of the headquarters in Veceriska causing extensive damage to the headquarters premises. We suspect that it was also Ferhet Haskic who threw the explosive device," signed, "Duty Officer in the Brigade, Ivan Budimir." I'm asking you about this document, 209A. Does it correspond to the events that actually took place?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: We received a report to this effect in the command of the Operative Zone. I'm familiar with the events and I'm familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the needs of this trial, let us look at things from the ethnic standpoint. This is a report of the Viteska HVO Brigade, which is a Croatian unit, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ferhet Haskic, is he a Muslim from Donja Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Ferhet Haskic is a Muslim living in Donja Veceriska. I think he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The command in Donja Veceriska, in front of which Haskic threw an explosive device, was that the local HVO command?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, the command of the local units in that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the Haskici and most of the Muslims and Croats in Donja Veceriska employed in the SPS ammunition factory? Were explosives readily available to, more or less, everyone in the village?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Let me explain. Within the territory of Vitez, there was an explosives factory, in which most of the inhabitants of Vitez municipality were employed. Due to this, explosives were readily accessible to most people who, especially when the combat operations started on the part of the army of Republika Srpska, would simply appropriate such explosives. Later on, these explosives, probably, were channelled in various ways among various groups of criminals, and the people who could gain possession of the explosives were linked together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this mean that, in addition to soldiers, civilians also had possession of explosives?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. We will distribute the document, but we will resume our work at 2.30. The hearing is now adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.58 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We'll resume our hearing. Could General Blaskic be brought in, please? (The accused entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I think that we have arrived to a point where you were presenting a new document. Can you hear me, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, that is correct. But I made an omission, and please allow me to correct it. What I have omitted was that we forgot to present Brigadier a bit more. We do not know what he did during the war and what was his education, so if you allow me now to spend a few minutes on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you please tell the Court, what did you do before the beginning of the war on the territory of the former Yugoslavia? What schools did you attend and what jobs did you hold?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I finished, as a civilian, the faculty for political sciences. My specialisation was in social work and defence, these were two different sections. Later on, I worked on civilian structures of defence for some 13 or 14 years. Out of my military education, I can say that I attended a school for reservists in infantry. This was not specialised military education. It was carried out during regular military service, an obligation I had as a Yugoslav citizen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your military service and that school for which I believe lasted for six months, did you become a member of a military unit before the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The programme of that school was to form in six months, reserve officers, for duties up until a company, and after that school, depending on how long your military service was. That depended on your education. If you had higher education you only went to the military for 12 months, and if not, for 15 months. So, I spent 12 months doing my military service. After that, I came back home and I worked in the structures of civilian defence, as I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, when did you prepare in defence from the aggression of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: When the war in Bosnia began, I worked in the municipal secretary for defence in Novi Travnik. In that capacity, in April 1992, I became a member of the HVO as an expert consultant at the municipal staff in Novi Travnik. Because of my experience, I could organise the units in the municipality of Novi Travnik. Since October 1992, I worked in the command of the Operative Zone with the headquarters in Vitez, and my mission was in the training, operational training department, where I was head of that department. After the Washington Agreement I became the Chief of Staff at Tomislavgrad, and I spent two years performing that duty. After the army of the federation had been established, I was appointed Chief of Staff of the 1st Guards Brigade in Mostar, a duty I still hold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain something else to the Tribunal? What were your duties in the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia? You said that you were chief operative officer?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: My duty as the head of the department for training operations was to organise the command, to carry out the commands, and prepare the carrying out of the commands, all the follow-up of the commands, also the training of the units. Also, I had to follow and monitor the situation at the defence lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now we can go on to the document we have mentioned before lunch break. Could the usher please assist us to distribute that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We have a problem with the transcript here. Brigadier Marin said that he was the Chief of Staff of the district, and in the transcript we have the brigade. This is not the same thing. The military district.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you repeat what your function was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Tomislavgrad, Chief of Staff of military district.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which includes various brigades?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is equivalent to corps.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document D210, 210A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you take a look at this document? I will read its main lines. It is dated the 16th of March, 1993, and it was written by the reserve members in Donja Veceriska. It says, "On the 16th of March, 1993 at 4 o'clock in the cafe, a meeting was held of the reserve force of the HVO of Donja Veceriska at which the following conclusions were made." Under one, "On the 16th of March, 1993, as of 18 hours, no acts of armed or other provocations, on the part of the HVO soldiers or the Muslim armed forces which serve the Croatian or Muslim population, will be tolerated." Two: "We shall do our utmost to preserve peace and tranquillity among the Croatian and Muslim people in this area, and we demand that the other side do the same." Three: "The Croatian and Muslim population will return to their household duties where, with regard to the structure of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna will not cause discord between the two peoples which have been inhabiting this territory for centuries. The reserve units for Donji Veceriska and the Muslim army shall establish control over the extremists from among both peoples." Five: "The reserve force of the HVO of Donja Veceriska, for its part, will do everything to prevent Donja Veceriska from becoming a cross-roads for resolving Croatian Muslim conflicts in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna." Six: "The Muslim army of Donja Veceriska will fill in all trenches in the interest of the further coexistence of the two peoples in this territory." Seven: "Unauthorised entry into other persons' yards is prohibited and anyone found in another person's yard will be arrested. Reserve force of the Donja Veceriska HVO." Tell me, first; do you remember these local negotiations, and was it a typical case that there would be conflicts at village level between two armed formations, or that there would be conflict between two villages at the local level?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Such activities regarding agreements, as it's stated in this letter, aren't known to me; but that happened as a result of intentions to diminish the tensions that had existed, the tensions which were caused by extremist behaviour, both in the BH army and the HVO. The most obvious example can be seen from the date of this document. This document was a result of a random checkpoint put up near Donja Veceriska. It was a case we mentioned before the break, maybe you remember the name of Haskic. Also, from the conclusions in this document, we can see that there were tensions that existed precisely between the armies organising villages, the members of the HVO and the BH army which can be seen from the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is another thing I would like to ask you. This text that starts "On the 16th of March, 1993, at 1700 hours, the reserve force met at the cafe," and then the name; is this a military way of taking decisions, or is it the democratic way of taking decisions which you mentioned existed in villages?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, this was that democratic way of taking decisions. They were really voting, whereas, normally it would be a different thing in an army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can a small unit in a small village make such conclusions? Is it a military way of doing things or more the way politicians do things?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Normally politicians would need to take such decisions, or the representatives of the civilian authority. But as the military and the civilian sides were intertwined, in the general interest of the security of the population, such documents were produced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could we have the next document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D211, D211A for the French version and D211B for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, we have now the document D211; would you please take a look at the document? Turn to the last page and could you tell us whether that is the signature of Colonel Blaskic and the seal of the Operational Zone, and can you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: This is the signature of General Blaskic and the seal is of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia. There is even my personal note here. What is said, what I wrote was across Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, yes, you added in your handwriting across Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to read out two or three key sentences from the order. On the 17th of March, 1993, Colonel Blaskic issues an order. "Treatment of persons inclined towards criminal and destructive conduct order." And then the preamble. It is addressed to all units, et cetera, within the Operative Zone. "In order to prevent the recurring, openly destructive conduct of individuals in HVO uniforms and the HVO armed formations insignia, and raise combat readiness, I hereby issue the following order." I will just quote point three, in order to save time. Point three: "Persons prone to disruptive conduct shall return their weapons, uniform and other equipment, and should be deleted from the wartime assignment lists and an appropriate assignment, according to the decree given to them." And the second paragraph of point four: "Commanders at all levels shall be responsible for covering conscripts prone to disruptive and criminal conduct, in particular, who have been recorded as such in the records of a platoon, company, et cetera." This document speaks for itself very clearly. It can be seen why it was written and what its message is. Could you please explain something to us? Colonel Blaskic says that the criminals have to be taken off the lists of HVO and assigned them adequately, give them adequate wartime assignments. Does it mean they will work in the working platoons, those who did not carry any weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the following page, point four, second paragraph speaks about the commanders who cover the criminals. Was it something that happened that normally a commander who should report it, he covers those people?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The reason for it was, I repeat, the units were formed in a village. In a village those people were parents, cousins, neighbours. That was one of the reasons why they were covered. But General Blaskic became aware of that, and he very precisely gave instructions to his subordinates stating that they had to be made responsible at a certain level. Furthermore, during his work, General Blaskic issued, also, oral orders of that kind. He insisted on briefings concerning the carrying out of such measures and commands, and he verified through me that we should seek the information and see how far were certain measures applied. However, a key problem in the application of these measures was that the commander of the Operative Zone, General Blaskic, did not have the instrument, did not have the physical strength in the form of an organised army to prevent such actions. So, simply we did not have such a force, a force organised in such a way to be able to prevent these actions. So, we had to go across various commands, and the only thing we could do was to transfer such a soldier from a war assignment into civilian protection, or assign him to work duty, which at that case was some kind of a sanction, because I already mentioned what it meant to wear a uniform in one's village. That was more or less the only measure we could take against those criminals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at the original in the Croatian language, and we have the initials "TBVS"; does it mean that Colonel Blaskic wrote that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, according to these initials, and according to the contents, I know that it was General Blaskic who wrote it himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we see here in the English and in the French versions it was SM, which would mean Slavko Marin; but we know this is a mistake in the translation, because we know it was Colonel Blaskic who wrote it. Could I ask the usher to bring a new document now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you the question now, Mr. Nobilo, because the Judges ask the questions after the examinations; but I would like to draw your attention to the point that you just mentioned. The initials that we have heard now, here, it is a bit curious, but you asked the question yourself; how come the initials were different? But please carry on, I'm sure we're going to talk about it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have to ask the translation, unit, Mr. President, which produced, as far as I know, these translations. I suspect they were working from a computer template, that is a form, and there are so many, there are many orders that this witness did author that would have SM on them, and they didn't change SM on their computer template to TB, which is very clear on the original. But we will have to ask them, quite frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, but nevertheless, I think that we should have a proof later on. But we had some typewritten error of that kind already yesterday, and this is something we cannot approach with neglect. But, please, Mr. Nobilo, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, on the original it is very clear, you can see very clearly who wrote it, and the translation unit is the one from this Tribunal; but on the original you see the letters TB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you got the original yourself, Mr. Nobilo? Have you got the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This is the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is a copy of the original. The Judges will, if necessary, ask to see the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we do not have an original, we also have copies of it. But you've got a copy. But when I'm speaking about the original, I mean the original in the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next document is marked 212, and D212A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, you spoke about the difficulties in the work of the civilian police, but also you spoke about the difficulties encountered by the military police. So, I should like to draw your attention to this document. Will you please see the name, Ivan Budimir and his signature; is that his signature?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to read some of the more important points in this analysis. "The second battalion command of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade provides an analysis of the work of the military police in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Battalion. "First: In Vitez, there is the regional military police, the municipal military police, the 4th Battalion of military police, and the civilian police. Secondly: We believe that there is no sphere of work. Three: Problems abound in the town, and in the entire municipality of Vitez, despite the presence of these four police forces. Four: Looting of cars, houses and socially owned companies, wounding in cafes, sabotage operations in towns, cafe killings, et cetera, are constant. Four: So far there have been six armed robberies; two Croats, one Serb and these Muslims. Five: Unauthorised barricades where there have been armed robbery have been springing up on a daily basis at night. Money, cars and other belongings are being taken away from them. Six: The police are not implementing orders regulating the opening hours of catering establishments, patrols of towns in the surrounding areas are either non-existent or infrequent. Seven: The police are not taking weapons from the soldiers, walking around town while off duty, and so on. Point eleven: The arrogant behaviour of the regional military police causes anxiety and affects the morale of our soldiers. According to our information, they receive a salary of one hundred Deutschmarks and participate in the night-time partying. For example, for New Year, I believe their work, especially in relation to the procurement of cars, their origin must be checked, as well. There is no date on this document, but according to the contents, when, roughly, could it have been issued in time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: According to my memory, this document could be placed sometime in February or March 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The New Year is mentioned, that is, the New Year from '92 to '93. Do you recall anything in particular that happened in the vicinity of the Vitez Hotel, near the command, for New Year's Day 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. I remember a very important event. It was important from the standpoint of the security of General Blaskic himself, namely, the persistence of General Blaskic, through written and oral orders, to combat crime, to introduce order and discipline in the units, to improve the overall levels of safety in all towns and settlements. Certain criminal groups felt endangered by his attitudes. On the 31st of December, 1992, that is, New Year's Eve, an attempt was made on the life of General Blaskic by a soldier who headed for his office, the office where he assumed General Blaskic was. Fortunately, he was not there. In the corridor between the operations centre, where I worked, and the room where General Blaskic would normally be during working hours in the command building, he threw in a hand grenade. He was intoxicated, and after some time, the security staff of the command post managed to apprehend the soldier, take him out of the building. He resisted, and in the skirmish, the soldier lost his life. I repeat, this testifies to the very difficult situation we were in, because, in spite of all we did and the resources we had and the organisation that was established, this was something that did not suit the interests of criminals, and they resorted even to such extreme measures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to this document. Do you recognise it as a document typical for the period? Did you see it in that period?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Such reports would reach the command of the Operative Zone, and they were the result of an oral command of the commander of the Operative Zone to analyse, in detail, the situation, the causes, in order to identify the ways and means for overcoming this difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can I ask for the usher's assistance?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you once again, do you recognise the signature of Ivan Budimir on the last page?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the initial of Mrs. Nada Budza, who was the typist.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document D213, D213A for the French version, and D213B for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, a significant event occurred, which is indicative of what you have been talking about, the attack of an armed group against a police station, then the attack on a prison, and the release of a prisoner. I will now read a part of that report, and then if you could refresh your memory and tell us what you still remember about this event, and does this report truthfully reflect the event that took place. So we have a report addressed to the Military Police Administration in Mostar on 1st March, 1993, and it says: "Information about the persons who organised an attack on MUP," that is, the civilian police, "and the military police in Vitez." I will just read some passages from this text. The second paragraph: "By operative means, I have ascertained that Gazibaric has been a participant in a number of robberies in which vehicles and other valuable goods, as well as large sums of money, were alienated. The motive for his protection is of a purely materialistic nature." Two paragraphs down: "On 26 February, 1993, Ferdo Gazibaric was arrested and brought to MUP in Vitez." The letters are very small, so it's rather difficult to read from my copy. "The commander of the military police," this is the second to last paragraph on page 1, "Zarko Andric, organised a meeting of the military police, at which he informed those present of the arrest of Ferdo Gazibaric and of the need to set him free in order to prevent his disclosure of other participants in these criminal acts." I'll leave out the next page. On page 3, the third paragraph from the top: "At this meeting, negative comments were made about the role of Busovaca and the personnel in Busovaca, who are the policy makers, while not taking any concrete steps to defend Travnik. Thus, they said that the prison was full of Croats from Travnik, Vitez, and Novi Travnik, but that there was no one from Busovaca, although they know that many persons from Busovaca are involved in the same acts as they." I'll leave out one paragraph, and the next one says: "About 50 persons with big trucks and a PAM, an anti-air machine gun, driven in from the front-line in Turbe, as well as a number of personal automobiles, took off around 1600 hours in the direction of Vitez. With their arrival in Vitez, they created an exceptionally tense situation, both among the HVO units and among the population. Andric and some other military policemen occupied the MUP building," that is, the civilian police, "and of the military police building and demanded from Commander Pasko Ljubicic that he personally participate in freeing the arrested Gazibaric, and all this under constant threat of the use of available firearms. Since Gazibaric was in the Kaonik prison in Busovaca, freeing him was carried out there. From the rooms of the Military Police of the 4th Battalion, communication was established with Colonel Blaskic in Kiseljak. The situation they found themselves in was described to him, as well as the consequences which could result if their demands were not met and armed conflict occurred. Blaskic's suggestion was to do all this without the use of force and without bloodshed. After Gazibaric was freed, this 'unit' went in the direction of Travnik with uncontrolled shooting and yelling." On the fourth page, second paragraph, it says: "The link is well-known which these individuals have established with criminals from among the Bosniaks. Throughout the conflict in Busovaca, this group collaborated intensively with Refik Linda, Ramiz Delalic, and Soso. Their collaboration was reflected in the resale of stolen vehicles and technical goods and the protection of individual criminals, Pero and Stipo Zujl, for whom there is a warrant out." The last two paragraphs: "What occurred reflects negatively among the Croatian population and is perceived as the powerlessness of the legal organs and institutions of the HVO to counteract crime and criminals. In the ranks of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they could hardly wait for this, and it is commented upon as an open clash among the divided HVO forces. They follow further developments with satisfaction and expect such further clashes, which influences their morale considerably, and they are offering their 'help.'" Brigadier, first, are you familiar with this report? Do you recognise the signatures?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Both the report and the events are familiar to me, and the signatures are authentic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Brigadier, what do you remember about that event? Did it occur in the way it is stated in this report or do you remember anything additional to this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The report fully and in detail describes the event that occurred and the situation itself. When this happened, I was in the command of the Operative Zone. I was carrying out my regular duties. I received the report or, rather, the command received this report, but it was so complex, as the report itself indicates, that we had to contact Commander Blaskic who was in Kiseljak. The report speaks for itself, and it confirms all that I have said so far with respect to problems of ensuring public law and order, how to provide citizens with the necessary degree of safety, and how to resist criminal groups and individuals who, as you see, had gained so much strength that they influenced the soldiers who were holding the defence lines against the Serb forces, who managed to get anti-air weapons, and who wanted to liberate a man who had committed a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Brigadier, is this indicative of the fact that the HVO, at the time, was a well-structured, modern army? Would such an occurrence be possible in such an army or does it show something else?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: These events, this kind of event in a well-structured and organised army can never and will never occur, but in the conditions under which we were living and preparing for war, this is a fact, and that is exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, under those conditions, when one system had collapsed and another had still not been developed, how could Blaskic simply, effectively, carry out his orders? What did he have to have to support him for him to impose those orders? Was it just sufficient for him to issue an order, or did he need something to else to make sure that those orders were implemented?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: In the situation in which we found ourselves at the time, it was no where near enough for an order to be issued to be sure that it would be carried out. However, General Blaskic, who always said in personal contacts and at morning briefings that our task was to build the structure and the organisation, he sought, in every possible way, to carry out his assignment. One of those ways was to use roundabout methods, and those were mostly persuasion, talking about the harmful effects such behaviour would have, pleading, and only after all of those efforts could he issue an order and expect it to be realistically carried out. Otherwise, it just didn't work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If Colonel Blaskic had, as an outsider, come to the area of Vitez with a logistic base and 200 soldiers armed to the teeth accountable to him, would he have been able to impose law and order and efficiency?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: My opinion is that he would, but he did not have logistics, nor the executive strength to prevent such occurrences. As you see, the police arrested a criminal and, automatically, both the military and the civilian police were blocked in their efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can I have the next document distributed, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D214, D214A for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read a few passages from this document for the military police battalion. It is dated the 2nd of February, 1993, and the note was made by Josipovic, and the stamp is of the military police in Mostar. Before I read it, I want to ask you whether you recognise the name Ivan Josipovic and the stamp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Ivan Josipovic was an employee in the 4th Military Police Battalion. The stamp is of the Command of the Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is an official note compiled on the 2nd of February, 1993 on the premises of the criminal investigations department of the 4th Military Police Department in Vitez concerning the explosion which occurred on 1st February, 1993. A commission consisting of the following members, Ivan Josipovic operative, Ilija Marjanovic, forensics officer, Vjeko Saric, mortar unit commander, went to the scene of the incident and established the following: The explosion occurred on the main Vitez-Travnik road, that is, at the intersection of the road leading to Vitez in the immediate vicinity of the Impregnacija administration building and the house of Devad Mujanovic. Tell the Court, Devad Mujanovic, is that a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these routine notes compiled by the police after the inquest where various explosions had occurred?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, because the police didn't have the required personnel, nor the resources, to carry out the criminal investigation work any better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the military police was selective? Did it do such an investigations when the damaged party was a Croat and did not carry out investigations when the damaged party was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I am not aware of any such practice, but the military police went to the scene wherever it could and whenever it had any report on such similar events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can I call for the usher's assistance again, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D215, D215A for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let us first identify the document. It is dated the 22nd of March, 1993. It is from the 1st Battalion of the Vitez Brigade signed by Mr. Bertovic. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I do know him personally, and this is his signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a short document, so I will read the most important parts. I want to know whether you remember this order and whether such orders were issued to other units by the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. The date is 22nd of March, 1993. "In view of the fact that in a couple of days (on Wednesday, 24 March, 1993) the Muslims will celebrate their biggest holiday, Ramadan Bajram, and in order to prevent any possible negative consequences, I hereby order: All the units from the 1st Battalion of the Viteska Brigade shall increase the vigilance of all unit members in the next couple of days, and especially during Bajram, and, with the same aim, shall also step up security measures through constant monitoring and increased patrolling." Brigadier, my first question: What was the reason for Anto Bertovic to give such an order to his soldiers in the battalion to increase security measures for the greatest Muslim holiday, the Ramadan Bajram?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this order was issued just immediately prior to the beginning of the mentioned holiday. It was issued because of awareness that the population was mixed in the villages, that there were armed members of both the Muslim and Croat ethnic groups, that is, of the HVO and the BiH army, and because we knew what this holiday meant for the Muslim people. In order to make it possible for them to celebrate this holiday, the battalion commander issued this order to his subordinates to act as indicated in this order. However, in addition to what I have already said, the date, the 22nd of March, 1993, which we shall probably be referring to later on in this testimony, there were certain events that occurred at the time which may have brought about some irrational behaviour by individuals on this holiday, which would have had far greater and graver consequences and which would have further heightened tension than if the same kind of incident occurred on a day which was not a holiday. That is why the commander issued this order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you can recall, was the initiative taken by Mr. Bertovic or did an initiative come from the Operational Zone and its command?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the commander Colonel, today, General, Blaskic issued an order to the brigades and that orally, while communicating with the commanders, he insisted that they applied these measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could I ask for the usher's assistance now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document D216, D216A for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, this is a report which I am going to give just in its basic outlines, and it speaks for itself, by the way. Could you please tell us whether you recall the events we have just mentioned, and this report speaks about the violence on the other side, that means by the BH army towards the HVO. This is the report. The report was written by the already mentioned Ivan Budimir from the Viteska Brigade. "On the 27th of January, 1993 in Kruscica, near Fatina vodica, and at the Vatrogasni dom in Stari Vitez, the following MTS were confiscated by the BH army." Brigadier, would you explain to the Court what "MTS" means?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, in military terminology, "MTS" is an acronym for materiel and technical equipment, which implies weaponry and all other technical equipment used in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will not read it all. Let me just mention the locations where these weapons were seized. In point 3, it says that in Gornji Vitez, a certain quantity of weapons were seized from regional military policemen; then under 4, also in Gornji Vitez; and 5, in Kruscica, a certain quantity of weapons were seized; also, in point 6. There's no need for me to list the weapons that were seized. Tell me, do you remember this event or, at least, parts of this event, and were there any such violent acts undertaken by either side as early as January 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Such events were happening, both in the BH army and in the HVO. The events from this report are known to me. The locations where they happened are also known to me, because these are locations where the BH army had its checkpoints. So they had their checkpoints at Fatina vodica and at Stari Vitez, and the quantities of armaments listed here are correct. I know that we had to deal with this problem in the following manner: The commander in Vitez, which was Colonel Mario Cerkez, contacted the commander of the 325th Brigade, and together they were solving these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can I ask for the usher's assistance with a new batch of documents?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D217, D217A for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, I will now read about this event. Could you tell us, first, can you recognise the signature of Mr. Budimir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just read the beginning, not all of it. "On the 27th January, 1993 in Kruscica, the regular shift change was carried out. Upon return from Kruscica, a tam minibus van was stopped at 12.30, and it was driven by Stipo Livancic and carrying all the members of the shift. It was stopped on its way to Kruscica. All the occupants were disarmed and the minibus van was confiscated." Then follows a list of the weapons. Do you remember this event and where was the shift coming from?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I remember this event and the location where they were disarmed. Everything that was taken from them was there at that checkpoint which was constantly held by the BH army members. This shift was coming back from the defence lines towards the army of Republika Srpska, and they were carrying back equipment and weapons to a small base which was at the Lovac Hotel at Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could we have the next document, now, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D218, D218A for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, here, this is a communiqué which was given by the press office in Novi Travnik and IPD from the Brigade Novi Travnik, which is information and propaganda activity, the IPD. I will only read the beginning. "Public announcement: Today, the 10th of February, 1993, in Novi Travnik, First of Maj Street at the Dura cafe owned by Dzorde Matovinovic. Zoran Jukic, also known as Juka from Novi Travnik, was killed while resisting the Novi Travnik HVO military police to bring him into custody for harassing and seriously wounding a citizen." Had you heard that public announcement in February 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this public announcement was transmitted through the local radio at Novi Travnik. The event itself happened at the cafe, the owner of which was a Serb, because of the deeds that were described here; and during the intervention of military police, Zoran Jukic was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And military police had intervened because he was mistreating a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, but that can be seen from the text, that is why I did not mention it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could I ask for assistance for the next document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D219, D219A for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, the last document, D218, was speaking about a killing by the military police --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, I was actually drawing the attention to the previous document, the one from which we had just read, and this is the basis for my next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, the previous document we have just quoted where Zoran Jukic was killed because he had mistreated a Muslim, has the date the 10th of February, 1993. The new document, D219, was written two days later on the 12th of February, 1993. Here it says "Report from the arrest of a member of the HVO. On the 6th of February, 1993 at 1.30 at Kruscica in front of the black house and by the members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Muslim armed forces the following soldiers were arrested of the 2nd Battalion," and then comes the list of the names. "According to witness statements, one of those making the arrest was from Kruscica and the other three were members of the MOS from Vranjska." Are you familiar with this event, and in the way it has been described in this report written in the original by Ivan Budimir by hand?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I am familiar with the event, the place where it took place, as well, and a number of those arrested, and I am familiar with the place Serna Kuce or black house, it is a building known by the locals as black house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I can ask for the next document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: First document is D220, and D220A for the English translation. The second document is D221 and D221A for the English translation. The third document is D222 and D222A for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, maybe it is the right moment now to make a break. Have you got other documents to distribute now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Not at the moment. These are documents that speak about discipline, and I would like to say something about the disciplinary measures, but we can do it after the break, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In that case, we will have a 20-minute break. Have you got other documents now, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I have another one D223 that I will have to distribute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please do it now and then we will make a break. Is this the last document now? Can we have the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In that case, we will have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume now. Please have the accused brought in. You may be seated. (The accused entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, just before the break you distributed a number of documents, I think two or three batches, the fourth or the fifth one has arrived. Yes, Mr. Dubuisson, four or five documents, so, you've actually used our absence to distribute more documents now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Documents D224, next to the number of the document is written A2. That document is the document D224, and D225 has got next to the number E8 written on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo. Before the break you distributed, to us, five different documents; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. President, and we are not going to go into the details of all of these documents, because they speak for themselves, but they represent the basis for me for a series of questions, so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Brigadier, you have had time during the break to look at documents. Can you tell us, first of all, whether these documents are authentic? And the second thing, what are these documents?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the documents speak about the application of the disciplinary measures in certain units which were in the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, Brigadier, what were the authorities of Colonel Blaskic, the commander of Operative Zone, in matters of discipline? And did he have any influence once crimes or misdemeanours were committed and the sanctions?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I will try and explain it now. We have seen that General Blaskic was constantly trying to structure the units and to diminish the number of incidents, that the army starts functioning as much as possible on military principles. In order to achieve that, Commander Blaskic used all his authority and he ordered the application of military and disciplinary matters in certain units. According to the regulations that were then existent and that regulated the situation in the HVO, the commander of an Operative Zone had the authority to issue disciplinary measures; but he could not start a criminal proceeding or perform anything else from the criminal code. The commanders of various units had similar authority. In order to achieve some results, the commander of the Operational Zone, Blaskic, formed a military disciplinary court at the level of the command of the Operational Zone, and he also instructed that in the brigade such military disciplinary tribunals be formed. Such military disciplinary tribunals had to carry out the disciplinary proceedings in those cases when commanders in the subordinate units made a disciplinary misdemeanour, or a breach of discipline. At the level of the command of the Operative Zone, a disciplinary military tribunal was established by the command of its commander, by order of its commander, and the closest collaborator of the general were in that tribunal. I was the deputy prosecutor at that disciplinary military tribunal, and we also had some cases, first of all, against the subordinates in our Operational Zone. In the brigade commands, there were also disciplinary military proceedings against those that were in their brigades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was responsible for the criminal prosecution of criminal offenders? Who was, in the chain of command, responsible? Which bodies were responsible for carrying out proceedings against criminal offenders?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was the military prosecutor's office. Some elements of that structure had been established, but I'm not familiar with the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the military prosecutor's office exist, and was there also a military court?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The military prosecutor's office and the military court, was it under the command of the Operative Zone, or was it organisationally part of the legal structure?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If the witness can answer the question without Mr. Nobilo suggesting the answer, I think it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have the feeling that Mr. Nobilo was just about to complete his question. Will you please finish your question, Mr. Nobilo? Was there a question that you haven't had time to answer? I'm a directing myself to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, then. Finish your question, Mr. Nobilo, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: The military prosecutor's office and the military court, was it under the command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, or was it part of the structure of the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The military court and the military prosecutor's office were not under the command of the commander of the Operative Zone, but they were part of the structure of the justice department of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These documents that you have had occasion to review; there are various types of reports having to do with disciplinary measures from D220 to D225; are these documents authentic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The documents are authentic, and they were issued on the basis of the orders of the commander of the Operative Zone, as can be seen from the document marked E8. Because the commander of the Operative Zone, in order to make sure that his order is being implemented in the field, would ask individuals by name what they had done for each individual disciplinary offence. This can be seen from the reports on the table which come from five different units that were part of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could the usher please distribute the next series of documents, which are also linked to disciplinary procedures, and the reports to the command regarding those disciplinary proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: In order to facilitate the work of the parties and you, Your Honour, Mr. President, and Your Honours, the documents have already been marked in the right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's perfect, Mr. Registrar. You can do that for all the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, will you take your time and look at each of these documents? Several more are in preparation with the registrar. Brigadier, these are reports by individual units on disciplinary measures issued and which reached the command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. These reports that you have before you, did you receive them in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, and are they authentic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: All these reports were received in the command of the Operative Zone, as can be seen from the stamp verifying receipt at the bottom. I was informed by the commander of these reports at a morning briefing when the assistant for personnel and legal affairs reported on the implementation of the orders on the basis of which individual commands sent back reports to the command of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please review a number of new ones. My question is the same. The documents speak for themselves. We will not read them. What is important for us is whether you remember these reports reaching the command of the Operative Zone and whether they are authentic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: These reports that I'm now holding also came to the command, and they are also authentic, and they arrived from specific units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, for the record, could we be told the first and last number of all these documents linked to disciplinary measures so that they may be referred to correctly in the record?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first set of documents was, D225 was the last one, then we come from 226 to 234; A, of course, for the English version. From 226 to 234.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: May I ask for the usher's assistance with a new document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document 235, 235A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document is brief. I will read it. It is addressed by the 111th XB Brigade from Zepce on the 11th of August, 1993, and it is addressed to Deputy Commander for IPD of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. It is headed "Request," and it reads: "Due to the specific position of the 111th XB Brigade and the lack of a military prosecutor's office and a military court in Zepce and the increase in the number of criminal offences, I hereby request urgent instructions on how to raise the issue of criminal responsibility and the determination of the competent court of our brigade. Deputy Commander Drago Ezgeta." What is this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the following should be pointed out: The area of Zepce was physically separated from the command post of the commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. One can infer from this request that the problem of military discipline and the problem of crime was not typical for the Lasva Valley alone. This problem was of general significance for the whole area. As a military prosecutor's office and a military court was in the Lasva Valley, it could not act in Zepce. The assistant for political and information activities of the 11th Brigade addressed our command, or rather his colleague, in terms of speciality, asking him to give him information about the implementation and instituting criminal proceedings for their brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell me, the stamp at the bottom, what does it signify? Is it the date when your command received it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, it is the receiving stamp. You will see it on all documents which were received by the command of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Next document, please. INTERPRETER: Interpreters would like to ask counsel to read more slowly, because there is no French translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 236, 236A for the French version, 236B for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a hand-written document, I will read only parts of it, and then put my question. The title of the document is "Appeal," obviously written by a soldier, and it reads: "I, Borislav Lovrenovic, son of Marko and mother Karta, nee/Sureta, am the father of four minor children and live in Nova Bila. I am appealing against the order by Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, and my prison term of 30 days in military prison." And then a few lines further down he says that he was a member of the Zuti special purposes unit, and says, "I did not participate in the attack on the police station in Vitez or in various other actions." So, I will not read on. Maybe I should read a little more. "I would also like to note that I did not take part in the Tuzla convoy, or in any other dishonest acts. I was there only a short time, and seeing that the whole burden of the group was being led by 10 or 15 young men, I went immediately to the command and asked for permission to leave the group. The commander, Mr. Ilija Nakic, gave me permission to leave the Zuti special purposes unit on 6 September, 1993." There are many errors, but what is this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: It is an appeal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it mean that you had a two-tier proceedings?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. According to the rules on military discipline, when a disciplinary measure is issued, the brigade commander could be appealed to by a soldier, as this case illustrates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brigadier, I should like to draw attention to the fact that this soldier is appealing against the command of Colonel Tihomir Blaskic. Who is he addressing his appeal to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: If the commander issues the order on a military sentence, then he addresses himself to the highest level of command, and that is the commander of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if the commander of the Operative Zone issues a punishment at the first level, who could he appeal to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: According to the rules and regulations then, this should be addressed to the main command of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this period were you cut-off from the main staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Hold on, let me think a moment. This was the period when there were attacks against military police? Yes, at that time we had already been cut-off from the main headquarters.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D237, D237A for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, can you please take a look at this order and can say whether it is authentic, whether there is Blaskic's signature there and a stamp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me what it looks like? It looks, to me, like a form of some kind.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: In order to implement the disciplinary measures at the highest level of quality, and given the inadequate training of commanders in particular units, the operative command staff, on orders of General Blaskic, compiled a standardised form, so that any disciplinary measures that were taken would be unified and so that any disciplinary measure could be issued accordingly. Such forms were also then distributed among the particular units for their use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Please, can we have the next document shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D238, D238A for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, this is a two-part document. There is a hand-written appeal and an appeals decision. Could you please review both parts of this document? I'm going to start with the second part, the hand-written appeal. This is Mato Biljaka from Kaonik Prison. This is where the prison was, and he is writing an appeal. He says: "Appeal to Mr. Tihomir Blaskic, Commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. Dear Colonel, since I received the order for detention lasting 30 days, I feel that my sentence is too harsh. Since I carried out every order on orders from the commander, often exposing myself to mortal danger, I do not deserve this punishment. I would like to ask you to lower the sentence, since I intend to get married on 12 December, 1993. Hoping that you will grant my appeal, I thank you in advance." And then submitting the appeal, Mato Biljaka. The first part of the document is the decision by Colonel Blaskic, and let me read it to you. "District Military Prison in Busovaca," this is in the Vitez command area, dated 24 December, 1993, and it's addressed to the District Military Prison in Busovaca where the man was serving his prison term. "I studied your appeal and I believe that in pronouncing the disciplinary measure, pursuant to Article 7 of the rules on military discipline, the commission of a punishable offence, which is prosecuted ex officio, and activities contrary to military regulations were taken into consideration and that the length of the pronounced disciplinary measure corresponds to the change in disciplinary violation. Pursuant to Article 47 of Rules on Military Discipline, I hereby pass the following decision: 1) I hereby deny the appeal of Mato (father's name Rudo) Biljaka, and consider the disciplinary measure to be founded." The signature follows "Colonel Tihomir Blaskic." Brigadier, I assume that you're not familiar with the handwriting of Mr. Biljaka, but you may recognise the signature of Mr. Blaskic, as well as the stamp of the command of the Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. I do recognise both the signature of Colonel Blaskic and the stamp of the Operative Zone Command, but I'm aware of several such decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on what you just said, would you conclude that Colonel Blaskic was the appeals instance in these legal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. This is an excellent example to confirm just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we have the next document shown to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D239, D239A for the French translation, and D239B for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, very briefly, is this Colonel Blaskic's signature and the stamp? Do you recognise that, too?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is another example of the form which you compiled for issuing disciplinary measures?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to point out another thing here. This measure is for 30 days of prison, and this is the maximum punishment that a commander of the Operative Zone could pass for a disciplinary infraction. You couldn't give any more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, that completes the questions in the area of disciplinary measures and competence of Mr. Blaskic. I would now like to pass on to another area which has to do with the structure of brigades. We are going to focus specifically on the brigade structures in Central Bosnia's Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D240, D240A for the French translation, and D240B for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, before we go into this document, I would like to point out that you frequently changed the organisational structures within the HVO. You talked about the crisis staffs, about the municipal headquarters, and now we come to the brigades. How do you explain that? What was the reason for it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The situation in which we found ourselves, the need to organise a quality defence against the Republika Srpska and the efforts of the commander of the Operative Zone to establish a military organisation which would operate on the basis and principles of a military organisation, all this required that we continuously search for the best modes of organisation in order to establish a chain of command, in order to come to an efficient defence and to have the highest level of command and control. It is through these efforts that this organisation was changing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what brigades were established in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone in November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: We can see from the document which brigades were established, but let me point out the following, which is what we're interested in here: The commander of an operative zone, when he made decisions about the establishment of brigades, he had to take into account the desire that every municipality wanted their own. Here we have that Usura was established Usura, and Travnik in Travnik, and so on. Later on, we shall see that not every town would be able to have their own brigade. So Zenica had its own brigade, and then for the municipalities Maglaj, Novi Sehir, Teslic, Komusina, Zavidovici, and Zepce had one with a seat in Zepce. Now, why do we have one for all these municipalities? Because with the exception of Zepce, all these municipalities were under Serbian control. Most of them were manned. The personnel was in Zepce. Then we have Kiseljak, Kresevo and Fojnica, they were all in Kiseljak, but later on we see that it was untenable, so that changed, and we had a brigade in Kiseljak. Then in Kakanj and Vares, that brigade also was changed, and the Jajce Brigade, which was in the Travnik barracks. This is how we envisaged it to be, because we thought that we would be able to keep the refugees from Jajce in Travnik. However, we did not succeed in that. All men of fighting age from Jajce, which, after the fall of Jajce, were driven out, the Croats, that is, they left the Lasva River Valley region. Also, here, there are certain deadlines imposed and some administrative matters which were essential for the establishment of brigades. Another important thing to mention here is that I took part in the implementation of this order by the commander, and earlier I said that we did not have a standardised structure. But those of us who knew something about organisation was tasked, by the commander, commensurate to our needs, to compile a manual on organisation of these brigades. As far as I recall now, these brigades were supposed to have about 2.800 soldiers, but I can tell you the actual numbers, the strength of these brigades, when we get to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are talking about the commanders and commands here. Was it possible, in the military hierarchy, if Blaskic ordered that such and such person was going to be the commander of such and such brigade, did this person need to consult someone else and receive somebody else's order?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that we had been in the war for almost a year, nothing changed on the ground. Still, with appointments of brigade commanders, the key role was played by the local political authorities with respect to brigades and with respect to subordinate units, which were still on the ground in villages, as we can see from this map. The organisation was still in place, as it was. So the key role with appointments had the villagers themselves. Such decisions would be taken in meetings of local communes and sometimes in the municipalities, and this would be then forwarded to the commander of this zone. And he would just formally confirm the appointment of such commander. Had he not done that, he would have had even more problems with the functioning of the system, and if he had done otherwise than what I have just said, he would have had even more problems locally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, the names of the brigades --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can you develop this more? What happens to the commander appointed from above when the community chooses another one? Are there two commanders then or what?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The commander of the Operative Zone, Colonel Blaskic, was aware of this situation, and he appointed commanders after consultations with the local authorities, so that we did not have cases of dual command. Had it ever happened, that would be a great disaster, because, at the time when we were establishing brigades, the pressure on the frontlines on the part of the Serbian troops was enormous, and we needed to keep those defence lines in place, as we had been trying since April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, can you tell me, on page 2, you see the signature and you see the stamp. Is this document authentic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. This document is authentic, and I said that I had taken part in its compilation and in its implementation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me move closer into this subject. When we talk about the brigade, the concept of the brigade, we think that this is a big, significant, mobile force. What is the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade in Vitez and Travnik? What did it represent in comparison to the units of the municipal headquarters? I'm sorry. In Vitez and in Novi Travnik, not Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the brigade, and we look at the organisation of the brigade, what is the difference between a brigade and a municipal headquarters? In practice, this was just a different name. So what used to be the municipal headquarters was now called a brigade. But due to all the problems, which I have mentioned, and the local situation, both in villages and municipalities, we were not able to comply with the standards which went along with the term "brigade." So that in all future considerations, if you want to have a real picture of the situation that we had, we had to bear in mind this fact. Let me repeat: We just renamed the municipal headquarters into brigades. The command, by structure, it was envisaged that it would have several officers who would be specialists, but the organisation, the structure on the ground, remained the same. We would have a company in a village of 30 or 50 people, and we would have the same units. We would still continue with the same tasks on the line of defence, as we had done in April of 1992, because we did not have the right conditions to deploy the units in a particular area where we could train them, where we could develop the command structure, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document compiled on 25 November, 1992, can you see whether it was addressed to the commanders of municipality headquarters? Is it to them that it was addressed? Were they the people who organised this brigade and who became their commanders?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. It is clear from the document that this is where this order went, and it is the presidents of these municipal headquarters that became commanders of the brigades. As I said, we tried to merge two municipal headquarters into a single brigade. Our basic task was to organise the defence against the Army of Republika Srpska. In Novi Travnik, we planned to organise one single brigade of Novi Travnik and Vitez, because that is where the front-line was against the Army of Republika Srpska. We wanted to have a quality defence. We wanted, also, to bring to a minimum all the shortcomings which we had in the organisation of this defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I just need the number of this document. I had not taken it down. Could you please tell me, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document D198. You're speaking of the map, I believe?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No. The command dated the 25th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry. In that case, this is document D240.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could I have the assistance of the usher for the next document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first document is marked D241, D241A for the French translation, and D241B for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, we have two documents here, the first document dated the 12th of March, 1993 where Colonel Blaskic issues an order that the organisation of the brigade and its monitoring is taken over by Mario Cerkez. The second document is the appointment of Mario Cerkez as the commander of the brigade. Could you tell us, in more detail, why that happened, and who did Blaskic have to reach an agreement with in order to issue this formal order?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Brigadier. Is this two documents, Counsel, or just one? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm asking the same question.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: These are two documents. I gave two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, but maybe there might be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just as Mr. Kehoe, I was not able to understand very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There's a small delay here.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Here is the second document which is marked D242, and there is the "A" and "B" version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can I continue now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let me repeat my question. Yes, we have got here two appointments on the 12th of March, and then in the second half of March 1993; could you tell us why a new brigade was organised, why so late, and who had decided that Mario Cerkez would be commander?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, when I was explaining the activities about the organisation of brigades, which were the results of the commands and orders we saw before these documents, I explained what the purpose of it was. However, our intentions, we were unable to carry them out. Two months after we issued the order we had to transform, that is, to modify that order and issue a different order mentioned under point 1, and saying that the organisation, supervision and coordination in all activities with the organisational brigade in Vitez, that those activities would be under Mr. Mario Cerkez, who was the commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade from Novi Travnik.
